sections.title: Using a shadow to mark the day
paragraphs: A shadow moves because the direction of incoming sunlight changes during the day. A vertical stick placed in the ground gives a simple way to observe this. The end of its shadow can be marked at intervals, and the marks can be connected to show how its position changes. The shadow usually changes in both direction and length. For that reason, a single measurement of length does not necessarily identify one moment. The same length may occur before and after the Sun reaches its highest point. An observer who also records direction can distinguish cases that would otherwise look identical.

The length depends on how high the Sun appears above the horizon. When the Sun is low, light arrives at a shallow angle and the shadow can reach far from the base of the stick. When the Sun is higher, the shadow is shorter. The ground needs to be considered as part of the arrangement. A sloping surface can alter the measured length and the position of the tip. If several observations are intended to be compared, a firm level surface helps keep that source of difference small. The stick should also remain in the same position throughout the observations.

The time at which the Sun reaches its highest position on a given day is often called local solar noon. It need not occur at twelve on a clock. A clock can be set to a common time shared across a wide region, while the Sun’s position at a given clock time depends partly on the place of observation. A region using the same clock time can contain locations where the shortest shadow occurs at different times. This distinction matters when interpreting an old description that refers to midday. The term might refer to a local event in the sky or to a time marked by the clock.

A sundial makes use of regular changes in direction. Its marks are arranged so a shadow indicates part of the day as it moves across them. The device has to be designed and oriented for the conditions in which it will be used. Moving a dial to another place or turning its base can change the relation between the shadow and the marks. A dial should therefore be checked in position rather than assumed to give the same reading wherever it stands. A well-placed dial can be read without a moving mechanism, but its accuracy still depends on the shape and arrangement of the parts.

The pattern of marks also changes with season. The path of the Sun across the sky is different at different times of the year. At a place with strongly varying seasons, the shortest shadow of a day can be much longer in one season than in another. An observer comparing the same shadow length across different months needs to know how the dates differ. Instead of using a single mark as a fixed guide to the hour, a study can record a series of lengths and directions on several days. The resulting collection shows which changes recur daily and which develop over a longer period.

Weather can affect how clearly the shadow is seen. A sharp edge is easier to mark than a broad patch under a cloudy sky. A record can therefore include a note about visibility and can distinguish uncertain marks from clear ones. When the Sun is partly hidden, a missing mark indicates a gap in the observation. It need not be interpreted as a sudden change in the path. If the study needs a precise position, it is better to repeat the reading under clearer conditions than to give a precise value to a mark whose edge was not visible.

A shadow record is most useful when the observer states what is being compared. The measurements can illustrate changes in the Sun’s apparent height, show the approximate sequence of hours or help compare dates. The same set of marks may serve several of these purposes, although the records needed for each are not identical. A guide to local time needs information about place and orientation, while a comparison of seasons needs reliable dates. Thinking about these requirements at the beginning makes the result easier to interpret. It also makes clear why the simplest instrument can still depend on a carefully planned observation.

sections.title: Turning loose wool into felt
paragraphs: A piece of felt can hold together even though it is not made by crossing threads in a woven pattern. It is formed from fibres that become entangled. To begin, the fibres can be spread in loose layers. The direction and thickness of each layer affect how the piece behaves as it forms. If most fibres point the same way, the material may change size differently in different directions. Alternating the direction of layers can help create a more even result. The first arrangement does not look much like the finished piece, but it sets limits on where the dense and thin regions are likely to appear later.

Wool fibres have a surface structure that affects how they move past one another. Under suitable conditions, repeated movement can cause them to become more firmly entangled. Water helps the fibres make close contact, and soap may be used to help wet and handle them. Gentle pressure at the start can settle the layers without moving large groups of fibres out of place. More vigorous movement can follow after the layers begin to hold together. If the initial work is too forceful, some parts may move away before they have joined. The result can be a thin patch that becomes visible only after the rest has become dense.

As felting continues, the loose layer usually becomes smaller and firmer. The change can be measured by marking the original size and checking the piece at several points during work. It may not shrink by the same amount in both directions. A maker who needs a piece to fit a particular object can test a small sample first. The sample is most informative if it is prepared with similar fibres and a similar arrangement. A measurement made from a different process may give a precise number without giving a useful estimate for this piece. The test is intended to connect the starting dimensions to the likely finished dimensions.

A maker can combine colours before the fibres are firmly joined. Adding a line of coloured wool on the surface may preserve a visible pattern. Adding colour through the thickness can give a different appearance at a cut edge. Some movement of the fibres during felting can soften the boundary between colours. That effect may be desired in one piece and unwanted in another. The design has to allow for the way the material changes instead of treating the original arrangement as a finished picture. Inspecting a small sample from the side can help show whether the colour occupies only the surface or continues into the body.

Felt can be made around a temporary barrier. A layer of wool on one side of the barrier can join with a layer on the other side around its edges. The barrier prevents the two surfaces from joining across the middle. After the outer form has become stable, an opening allows the barrier to be removed. The result can be a hollow object without a seam running around its widest part. The method depends on leaving a route for removal and on keeping the edges thick enough to hold together. A barrier that is easy to place may be difficult to remove if the opening is too small.

After the fibres have joined, washing and drying can change the appearance and feel of the piece. Residual soap can affect the way a dry surface feels. A maker may rinse it and arrange the material in the desired shape while it dries. Pressing a wet piece flat can be useful for a panel, but would be inappropriate for a hollow form that needs to keep its volume. The final treatment should follow the intended use. A stiff wall and a soft pad can both be successful pieces of felt, although a test that compared them solely by firmness would wrongly treat one result as inferior.

The work becomes easier to repeat when the maker records the steps that produced a useful result. Useful notes can include fibre direction, the starting size, the size after shrinkage and the point at which the layers first held together. Such notes do not remove the need to inspect the material during the next piece. They provide a basis for deciding where a change occurred. If the same design becomes thinner when a different wool is used, the record makes it possible to compare the arrangement and the handling before attributing the difference to the wool alone. It turns a finished object into evidence about the process.

sections.title: What makes a prediction possible to test?
paragraphs: A prediction connects an account of how something works with an observation that has not yet been made. It becomes easier to test when the observation can be described before the result is known. A person might predict that a change to a workshop will improve its operation. That claim leaves several choices open. It could refer to the amount produced, the time spent on a task or the number of defects. Specifying the intended outcome and the period of observation allows another person to see whether the result meets the prediction. The writer treats this specification as part of the claim, rather than as a detail that can always be added later.

A test needs a way to distinguish the proposed effect from other changes. If a new tool is introduced at the same time as a new kind of job, a change in the measured outcome can have more than one cause. A comparison could use similar jobs before and after the introduction, or could observe two groups that use different tools at the same time. Each arrangement has limits. Earlier jobs may differ in ways that were not recorded, while two simultaneous groups may have different experience. A useful report identifies these limits because they affect what can be concluded even when the prediction and the observed result agree.

The direction of the prediction can sometimes be stated more clearly than its size. An explanation might predict that an object will cool faster under one condition without predicting exactly how much faster. That can still be tested, provided the observations can distinguish a real difference from ordinary variation. A small change that is within the resolution of the instrument will be hard to detect. In that case, failing to observe the difference does not decide whether the explanation is correct. The test may simply be unable to distinguish the relevant possibilities. Designing a useful test therefore includes thinking about what the method would be able to reveal.

An observation may also agree with more than one explanation. Suppose several accounts predict the same change when a particular input is increased. Observing that change can support their shared expectation without telling an investigator which account is better. A more informative test would ask where the accounts differ. They might predict different results when the input is decreased, or when another condition is held fixed. The writer favours seeking such points of difference before collecting the data. Otherwise, a successful prediction can appear to settle a dispute that the test was never capable of resolving.

Unexpected results are often treated as problems, but they can also show that the original conditions were not understood. An instrument may have failed, the procedure may have been carried out differently from the plan, or the proposed account may require revision. A single disagreement does not immediately distinguish these possibilities. Checking a recording of the procedure can reveal whether the intended test occurred. Repeating the observation with an independently checked instrument can address a different possibility. If the result remains unexpected after those checks, the investigator has stronger reason to consider whether the explanation itself needs to change.

There is a useful distinction between improving an account and making it impossible to test. An account can be revised to include a condition that was genuinely overlooked. That revision can lead to further predictions about when the effect should and should not occur. A change that merely explains every possible outcome after it happens offers less help. Readers need to know whether a new condition was proposed before the result or was introduced to explain it afterwards. The latter can be a good starting point for future work, provided it is treated as a new proposal whose consequences still have to be tested.

A record of predictions and observations lets others inspect the route from an explanation to a conclusion. It should show what was expected, which outcomes would have counted against the expectation and how the comparison was carried out. It can also identify outcomes the test could not distinguish. This record is valuable even when the result is inconclusive. It makes it possible to improve the next test without treating an uncertain result as proof for either side. The aim is a sequence of comparisons in which each step makes the alternatives clearer. A single successful forecast is one part of that sequence rather than its endpoint.
